title: The Sharpe Pint: Ceasefires, Hawks, and the R&D Illusion

opening_mood.text: Good morning. Grab a strong coffee—or something stronger, depending on how your portfolio handled the long weekend. While London was enjoying a rare spot of Bank Holiday sunshine, the rest of the world was busy shifting the tectonic plates of global finance. From a new regime at the Federal Reserve to a high-stakes game of chicken in the Persian Gulf, we have got you covered. Let us get you sharp for the desk.

content.text: 1. The Strait of Hormuz: A Fragile Ceasefire and $97 Brent

The US and Iran have reportedly hammered out a tentative 60-day ceasefire extension framework to reopen the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, which has been choked off since late February. Under the proposed deal, Iran would have 30 days to clear the sea mines it laid in the strategic waterway in exchange for the US lifting its blockade on Iranian ports and granting temporary sanctions waivers for oil sales. Brent crude immediately slid nearly 6% to around $97 a barrel on Monday. However, the optimism was quickly tempered on Tuesday morning after US Central Command launched fresh 'self-defence' strikes against Iranian mine-laying boats and missile sites, and President Trump posted on Truth Social that it is 'a great and meaningful deal, or no deal.'

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most critical energy chokepoint, carrying roughly 25% of seaborne oil and 20% of global LNG. The closure has been a massive stagflationary shock, driving up shipping costs and keeping central banks on high alert. Any progress toward reopening is a massive relief valve for global supply chains, but the fresh military strikes show just how fragile this 'ceasefire' actually is.

The City angle: For macro desks and asset managers, this is the ultimate volatility play. If the deal holds, expect a sustained drop in crude, which would take some of the heat off global inflation and give central banks room to breathe. If it falls apart, we are back to square one: $100+ oil, supply chain chaos, and a prolonged risk-off environment.

What to say at the pub: 'Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is the best news the global economy has had in months, but trading the headline is a minefield—literally. One Truth Social post or a stray drone strike in the Gulf, and we're right back to $110 Brent.'
2. The Warsh Era Begins with a Hawkish Twist

Kevin Warsh was officially sworn in as the 17th Chairman of the Federal Reserve on Friday, promising a 'reform-oriented' shakeup at the central bank. But the real firework came from Fed Governor Christopher Waller. In a dramatic pivot, Waller—previously one of the FOMC's more dovish voices—declared that the Fed should immediately axe its 'easing bias' from its policy statement. With April's preferred inflation measure hitting a hot 3.8%, Waller warned that 'inflation is not headed in the right direction' and that a rate hike is now just as likely as a cut. Traders are now pricing in a 70% chance of a rate hike by the end of the year.

Why it matters: The market had spent the early part of the year fantasising about rate cuts. Waller's pivot, combined with Warsh's reputation as a hard-nosed inflation hawk, has completely rewritten the script. The 'higher-for-longer' narrative is dead; we are now firmly in 'higher-for-even-longer, and maybe even higher' territory.

The City angle: Fixed income desks are feeling the squeeze, with short-dated Treasury yields edging up. For credit analysts and debt capital markets (DCM) teams, this means refinancing costs are going to remain painfully high. If you're interviewing, understand how a hawkish Fed impacts corporate debt serviceability and equity valuations—growth stocks are particularly vulnerable to a rising discount rate.

What to say in an interview: 'Waller's pivot is a massive regime shift. By removing the easing bias, the Fed is telling the market that the inflation floor is much stickier than anticipated. With Warsh at the helm, the bar for any future rate cuts is now incredibly high, and we have to seriously model the impact of another 25-basis-point hike on leveraged balance sheets.'
3. Nvidia's $81.6B Blowout: When 'Great' is the New 'Average'

Nvidia dropped its Q1 FY2027 earnings, and the numbers were, as usual, absurd. Revenue hit a record $81.6 billion (up 85% year-over-year), beating Wall Street expectations of $78.8 billion. Data center revenue alone reached $75.2 billion. To sweeten the deal, CEO Jensen Huang announced a massive new $80 billion share buyback and hiked the quarterly dividend from $0.01 to $0.25. Yet, the stock fell about 1.5% in after-hours trading.

Why it matters: When a company has a $5 trillion market cap, beating expectations is no longer enough—you have to absolutely demolish them. The muted share price reaction suggests that the market has fully priced in the AI infrastructure buildout. The narrative is shifting from 'how fast can they grow?' to 'how long can this capital expenditure cycle actually last?'

The City angle: For buy-side analysts, the massive $80 billion buyback is a fascinating signal. It suggests that Nvidia is generating more cash than it can physically redeploy into R&D or supply chain capacity. As one analyst put it, we are watching a hypergrowth story mature into a cash-returning giant in real time.

What to say at work: 'Nvidia's buyback is the real story here. When a tech pioneer starts returning that much capital to shareholders, it's a sign that the hypergrowth phase is maturing. It's still incredibly bullish, but it's a different kind of bullish—one focused on cash generation rather than just speculative multiple expansion.'
4. The K-Shaped Consumer: Retail Giants Reveal Financial Fatigue

First-quarter retail earnings from US heavyweights Walmart and Target have exposed a stark, K-shaped divide in consumer health. While both retailers managed to beat revenue estimates, their stock prices took a beating—Walmart fell 7.3% and Target dropped 3.9%. Executives warned that the temporary boost from early-year tax refunds is fading, and lower-income consumers are showing distinct signs of 'financial fatigue' under the weight of persistent inflation and high interest rates. Target also spooked investors by announcing a massive $5 billion capital expenditure plan for supply chain upgrades and store remodels.

Why it matters: Retail earnings are the ultimate diagnostic tool for the real economy. The message here is clear: the consumer is running out of steam. While higher-income shoppers are still spending, the lower-income demographic is trading down or cutting back entirely. This makes the Fed's hawkish stance even more of a tightrope walk—raising rates to fight inflation could push an already fatigued consumer over the edge.

The City angle: For equity research and consumer-focused private equity, the play is all about defensive positioning. Companies with strong private-label offerings (like Walmart) are better insulated than discretionary retailers. In interviews, use this to discuss the 'K-shaped recovery' and how macro pressures filter down to corporate margins and inventory management.

What to say in an interview: 'The retail earnings show that the consumer cushion is officially gone. Walmart and Target's results prove that the lower-income consumer is tapped out, and the boost from tax refunds was just a temporary band-aid. Discretionary spend is going to face a very tough second half of the year.'
5. Next Boss Warns of a 'Dramatic Fall' in UK Entry-Level Jobs

Lord Wolfson, the long-standing CEO of retail giant Next, has sounded the alarm over a 'dramatic fall' in the number of entry-level jobs in the UK. Wolfson revealed that Next now receives an average of 19 applications for every shop floor vacancy, up from 10 just two years ago. His comments coincide with a new report from the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) showing that youth employment in the UK has fallen by 4.3 percentage points over the last three years—a decline approaching the levels seen during the 2008 financial crisis and the pandemic. Wolfson also warned that the government's upcoming ban on zero-hours contracts would make hiring even more difficult for retailers.

Why it matters: Youth unemployment is a lagging indicator of economic health, but a doubling of job applicants suggests a severe structural mismatch in the UK labor market. The upcoming Employment Rights Act, which aims to ban zero-hours contracts, is designed to protect workers but may have the unintended consequence of causing corporates to freeze hiring altogether to avoid rigid labor liabilities.

The City angle: For UK-focused equity analysts, this is a major warning sign for domestic discretionary spend. If young people can't find work, high-street retail, casual dining, and entertainment sectors are going to suffer. It also highlights the regulatory risks of the new Labour government's labor reforms on corporate operating margins.

What to say at the pub: 'When the CEO of Next says entry-level applications have doubled, you know the UK jobs market is in trouble. Banning zero-hours contracts sounds great on paper, but in reality, it's just going to make corporates even more risk-averse when it comes to hiring young staff.'
6. Rachel Reeves' 'Buy British' Mandate for AI and Infrastructure

UK Chancellor Rachel Reeves has issued a direct mandate to cabinet colleagues, instructing them to prioritize British companies for government contracts in four key sectors: shipbuilding, steel-making, energy infrastructure, and artificial intelligence. Under new procurement guidance, these four areas will be officially designated as 'critical for national security,' allowing the government to bypass standard international bidding processes to support domestic industry.

Why it matters: This is a massive protectionist shift in UK economic policy, mirroring the 'Buy American' provisions of the US Inflation Reduction Act. By tying AI and energy infrastructure to national security, the Treasury is attempting to stimulate domestic high-tech manufacturing and prevent critical IP and infrastructure from being outsourced overseas.

The City angle: For investment bankers and venture capital firms, this is a major catalyst. UK-based AI startups and defense/infrastructure contractors just got a massive competitive moat. Expect a flurry of deal activity and capital raises in these sectors as companies position themselves to capture lucrative government contracts.

What to say in an interview: 'Reeves' 'Buy British' mandate is a clear pivot toward economic nationalism. By classifying AI and energy as national security assets, the UK is trying to build its own sovereign tech ecosystem. It's a huge boost for domestic defense and tech firms, but it could raise procurement costs for the taxpayer in the long run.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: Coming back from a three-day weekend (with both London and New York closed on Monday for the Spring Bank Holiday and Memorial Day), City traders have been greeted by a classic geopolitical 'three steps forward, two steps back' routine. Over the long weekend, a wave of optimism swept through the markets after President Donald Trump declared that peace negotiations with Iran were 'proceeding nicely'. That sent Brent crude tumbling over 7% on Monday to slide below $97 a barrel, while WTI fell to around $91.65. But just as everyone was preparing to price in a clean resolution, the US military launched overnight 'self-defence' strikes in southern Iran, targeting missile launch sites and mine-laying vessels. It is a sharp reminder that in geopolitics, the ink is never dry until the ink is actually dry.

This overnight escalation has put the immediate 'peace trade' on a brief pause. European equities opened on a somewhat soggy note on Tuesday, with Germany's DAX down 0.7% and France's CAC 40 shedding 0.9%, while the FTSE 100 managed a 0.7% gain as it played catch-up from Monday's closure. Meanwhile, US equity futures are still holding onto green territory, with S&P 500 futures up 0.6% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq leading the charge up 0.8%. The message from the equity desk is clear: investors are desperate to look past the military friction and focus on structural tailwinds, but the bond and FX desks are playing a much more cautious hand.
The Cross-Asset Read: What Markets Are Really Saying

If you are talking to colleagues today or heading into an interview, do not just say 'oil fell and stocks are mixed'. The real action is happening under the surface, where several key themes are playing out across asset classes:

items: The Warsh Era Begins with a Hike: Kevin Warsh was officially sworn in as the new Federal Reserve Chair on Friday, replacing Jerome Powell. Despite Trump's vocal demands for lower interest rates, the bond market is betting that Warsh's first major move will be a rate hike. The CME FedWatch Tool is now pricing in a 70% chance of a rate hike by December, with the market fully pricing in a quarter-point move from the current 3.50%-3.75% target range for the first time. The 'higher-for-longer' narrative has officially found its second wind.

Semiconductors as the Ultimate Equity Safe Haven: While geopolitics remains messy, the AI and chip cycle continues to act as the market's ultimate cheat code. South Korea's Kospi index surged nearly 3% overnight to hit an intraday record, driven by massive foreign inflows into tech. That momentum has carried straight into US premarket trading, with Micron Technology jumping 4.9% (helped by Trump calling the company 'great' at a weekend rally), Arm Holdings up 3%, and Marvell Technology rising 5.4% ahead of its Q1 earnings release on Wednesday.

Gilt Yields and BoE Caution: In the UK, 10-year Gilt yields have been flirting with the 5.06% mark, driven by political uncertainty and stubborn producer prices. Even though headline CPI recently cooled to 2.8%, Bank of England MPC member Megan Greene warned that central banks cannot simply dismiss supply shocks from the Middle East as temporary. The BoE is highly likely to keep rates on hold for longer as domestic growth fades.

FX Reversals and Rupee Pain: The US dollar, which slipped on Monday's initial peace optimism, has clawed back some ground on Tuesday following the overnight strikes. The euro-dollar cross touched 1.1653 on Monday before retreating back to the 1.1630 level. Meanwhile, the Indian Rupee took a direct hit from the geopolitical volatility, weakening by 47 paise to settle provisionally at 95.73 against the greenback as oil prices bounced off their Monday lows.

content.text: The bottom line for your morning catch-ups: the equity market is behaving as if a full Middle East peace breakthrough is already signed and sealed, while the bond market is quietly preparing for a more hawkish Fed under Kevin Warsh. If you are looking for a smart talking point today, point out this divergence. Equity investors are pricing in the best-case scenario for growth, but fixed-income desks are looking at sticky energy costs and a new Fed Chair who is highly unlikely to bow to political pressure for premature cuts.

content.text: The R&D Capitalisation Illusion (or Why Your Favourite Tech Stock Isn't Actually Asset-Light)

Imagine you are looking at a hot SaaS business or a biotech firm. The numbers look spectacular: minimal factories, barely any office space, and a Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) of 50%. You think you have found the next compounding miracle. But there is a catch. Traditional accounting treats Research & Development (R&D) as an immediate operating expense, like office snacks or electricity. In reality, R&D is a long-term investment. By expensing it immediately, accounting rules make these companies look far more asset-light than they actually are. To see the true economic picture, sophisticated investors capitalise R&D.
The Concept: Capitalising R&D

Under US GAAP, companies must expense 100% of their R&D costs in the year they occur. Under IFRS, research is expensed, but development costs can be capitalised once a product is commercially viable. This creates a massive comparability headache. To fix this, analysts treat R&D exactly like Capital Expenditure (CapEx). Instead of letting R&D hit the income statement as a massive operating expense, we remove the R&D expense from the income statement (boosting operating profit), create an Intangible R&D Asset on the balance sheet (increasing Invested Capital), and amortise that R&D asset over its useful life (typically 3 to 10 years), charging that amortisation back to the income statement.
A Simple Numerical Example

Let us look at SaaS-y Software Ltd. Under traditional accounting, they have Revenue of £100m, Operating Expenses (excluding R&D) of £50m, and R&D Expense of £30m. This leaves them with an Operating Profit (EBIT) of £20m. If their traditional Invested Capital (physical assets and working capital) is £40m, their traditional ROIC is a stellar 50% (£20m / £40m).

Now, let us capitalise their R&D. Assume R&D has a 3-year useful life, and the company has consistently spent £30m a year. The accumulated unamortised R&D asset on the balance sheet is £60m. To adjust, we add back the £30m R&D expense and subtract £20m of R&D amortisation, giving us an Adjusted EBIT of £30m. We then add the £60m R&D asset to the traditional £40m, giving us Adjusted Invested Capital of £100m. The Adjusted ROIC is now 30% (£30m / £100m). The business is still highly profitable, but the illusion of a 50% ROIC is gone. It actually requires a massive amount of intellectual capital to keep the lights on.
Why This Matters in Asset Management

If you do not adjust for this, you will misprice businesses. Michael Mauboussin, the legendary strategist at Morgan Stanley, has written extensively on how failing to capitalise intangibles leads to the erroneous conclusion that asset-light businesses have infinite returns. When you capitalise R&D, you get a much clearer picture of true economic moats (is the company earning high returns on all capital, or is it just running on an expensive R&D treadmill?) and reinvestment rates (aligning your DCF growth assumptions with the actual capital required to achieve them).
Common Beginner Mistakes

items: Thinking it changes cash flow: Capitalising R&D does not change a single penny of actual cash flowing in or out of the business. Free Cash Flow remains exactly the same; we are simply shifting where the cash outflow is classified.

Using a one-size-fits-all asset life: Amortising R&D over 5 years for a fast-moving mobile gaming company makes no sense when their games have a 12-month shelf life. Conversely, a pharmaceutical drug might have a 10-to-15-year useful life. Match the amortisation period to the economic reality.

content.text: How to Ace This in an Interview

If a buy-side interviewer asks how you would compare the profitability of a US software company and a European software company, do not just talk about EBITDA multiples. Hit them with this: I would start by standardising their R&D accounting. US GAAP forces companies to expense R&D, while IFRS allows capitalisation of development costs. To get a true apples-to-apples comparison of their operating efficiency and ROIC, I would capitalise the R&D for both. I would add back the R&D expense to EBIT, subtract an estimated R&D amortisation based on industry-specific asset lives, and add the capitalised R&D asset to the balance sheet to calculate an adjusted Invested Capital and ROIC.
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

Everyone raves about how tech giants are asset-light miracles. But if you actually capitalise Meta or Microsoft’s R&D and sales-and-marketing investments like Mauboussin does, their ROIC drops significantly. They are not asset-light; they are just physical-asset-light. Their intellectual capital requirements are massive—they just hide them in the operating expenses.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Idea: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for Option Pricing

Imagine you have built a shiny new deep learning model to price exotic options. It is fast, it is modern, and it is trained on mountains of historical data. But then you stress-test it, and it starts spitting out prices that violate basic financial laws—like pricing a call option below its intrinsic value, or implying a negative probability density. Your model is like a brilliant mathematician who has never heard of gravity. Standard neural networks are data-hungry black boxes; they can fit historical option prices, but they do not naturally respect the laws of financial physics, such as the Black-Scholes partial differential equation (PDE) or no-arbitrage constraints.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve this by embedding the governing PDE directly into the neural network's loss function. Instead of just learning from labeled data (which is often scarce or noisy for exotic derivatives), the network is trained on 'collocation points'—randomly sampled coordinates of stock price S and time t. We force the network to satisfy the Black-Scholes PDE at these points by penalising any deviation from the PDE in the loss function. This turns a pure curve-fitting exercise into a 'grey-box' model that is mathematically guaranteed to respect financial theory.
The Finance Example: Solving the Black-Scholes PDE

In quantitative finance, pricing complex, high-dimensional exotic options (like multi-asset American or path-dependent Asian options) using traditional numerical methods like finite differences or Monte Carlo is computationally brutal. Finite differences suffer from the 'curse of dimensionality' as the number of underlying assets grows, while Monte Carlo is slow and struggles with early exercise features. PINNs offer a mesh-free alternative that scales much better to high dimensions. Even better, because PINNs are built on deep learning frameworks, we can use automatic differentiation to calculate the Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta) exactly, without needing noisy finite-difference approximations.
Mini Technical Example: PyTorch Implementation

Here is how you construct the custom loss function for a Black-Scholes PINN in PyTorch. We use torch.autograd.grad to compute the partial derivatives of the network's output (V) with respect to its inputs (S and t), and then compute the PDE residual.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class BlackScholesPINN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 40),  # Inputs: Spot Price (S) and Time (t)
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(40, 40),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(40, 1)   # Output: Option Price (V)
        )
        
    def forward(self, S, t):
        # Concatenate S and t to pass through the network
        return self.net(torch.cat([S, t], dim=1))

def compute_pde_loss(model, S, t, r, sigma):
    # Enable gradient tracking for inputs to compute derivatives
    S.requires_grad_(True)
    t.requires_grad_(True)
    
    V = model(S, t)
    
    # First-order derivatives using PyTorch autograd
    V_S = torch.autograd.grad(V, S, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(V), create_graph=True)[0]
    V_t = torch.autograd.grad(V, t, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(V), create_graph=True)[0]
    
    # Second-order derivative (d2V/dS2)
    V_SS = torch.autograd.grad(V_S, S, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(V_S), create_graph=True)[0]
    
    # Black-Scholes PDE Residual: dV/dt + 0.5 * sigma^2 * S^2 * d2V/dS2 + r * S * dV/dS - r * V
    pde_residual = V_t + 0.5 * (sigma**2) * (S**2) * V_SS + r * S * V_S - r * V
    
    # We want this residual to be as close to zero as possible
    return torch.mean(pde_residual**2)
The Paper Angle

The foundational concept of PINNs was introduced by Raissi et al. (2019). In finance, researchers have extended this to high-dimensional option pricing. For instance, a thesis from ETH Zurich by Ramy Tanios, titled 'Physics informed neural networks in computational finance: High dimensional forward & inverse option pricing' (2021), demonstrated that PINNs can solve option pricing PDEs in high dimensions where traditional finite difference methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality and become completely intractable. The paper also shows how PINNs can be used for 'inverse problems'—such as backing out the market's implied volatility function directly from observed option prices.
The Interview & Coffee-Machine Conversation Angle

If you are in an interview for a quant research or model validation role, this is a brilliant topic to bring up when asked about how to combine machine learning with traditional quantitative finance. Instead of treating ML as a pure black-box curve-fitter, PINNs represent a 'grey-box' approach. You are using neural networks as universal function approximators, but forcing them to respect the laws of financial physics (no-arbitrage, PDEs). It shows you understand both modern deep learning and classical stochastic calculus, rather than just blindly importing scikit-learn. It is also a great discussion point for how to compute exact Greeks using automatic differentiation instead of bumping inputs and recalculating.
The Risks & Limitations

While elegant, PINNs are notoriously difficult to train. The loss function is a multi-objective optimization problem (balancing the PDE residual loss with the boundary condition loss). If the weights of these losses are not balanced correctly, the network can easily get stuck in trivial local minima (e.g., outputting zero everywhere). Furthermore, PINNs still require a specified PDE. If your underlying model assumptions are wrong (e.g., assuming constant volatility when the market is in a regime of stochastic volatility), the PINN will beautifully and precisely solve the wrong equation. It is a garbage-in, garbage-out problem, just with a much shinier engine.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Paper: MadEvolve: Evolutionary Optimization of Trading Systems with Large Language Models

If you have spent any time in a quant fund or on a trading desk recently, you have probably heard someone mutter about 'agentic AI' or 'LLMs writing code'. Most of it is vaporware—junior developers asking ChatGPT to write a basic Bollinger Band script that gets eaten alive by transaction costs. But a new paper published on arXiv (21 May 2026) by researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Event Horizon Labs actually does something clever. They took an open-source evolutionary framework called MadEvolve—originally built to solve complex problems in computational cosmology—and set it loose on quantitative trading.
Why This One Matters

Most attempts to use LLMs in trading fail because they treat the model as a predictor ('Hey Claude, where is Bitcoin going next?'). MadEvolve treats the LLM as an algorithm designer. It sets up an evolutionary loop where the LLM writes Python code for trading strategies, runs backtests, evaluates the results, and mutates the code over hundreds of generations to find better strategies. Crucially, it solves the classic 'dumb LLM' problem by using a nested architecture: the LLM only proposes the structure of the code (e.g., adding a new momentum feature), while a traditional mathematical inner loop handles the boring parameter tuning (like calibrating the exact lookback windows).
The Setup & The Results

The researchers tested the framework on BTCUSD 1-minute candle data from 2022 to late 2025. To keep things honest, they did not let the model trade in a frictionless fantasy world. They forced it to use passive limit orders, made decisions once per minute, and slapped on a realistic market impact penalty (using the Bouchaud impact model) to stop the AI from sizing its positions to infinity. Here is what happened:

items: Out-of-Sample Performance Boost: On the held-out test set (2025 data), the evolved strategy boosted the Sharpe ratio from a baseline of 3.82 to 4.45, and increased impact-adjusted PnL from $47k to $271k.

Stateful Logic Discovery: Instead of just tweaking numbers, the LLM actually evolved complex, stateful logic. It replaced a basic stateless threshold rule with a dynamic signal-processing rule that factored in momentum, inventory levels, and trade urgency.

A Shift in Style: Interestingly, the evolved strategy's win rate actually fell from 60.1% to 55.1% out-of-sample. The AI did not get 'smarter' at predicting every tiny move; instead, it learned to cut marginal, low-conviction trades and size up to capture larger, fat-tailed moves.

content.text: The Million-Dollar Question: Is It Just P-Hacking?

Every quant in the pub is going to ask this. If you run an evolutionary algorithm long enough, you will eventually find a strategy with a high Sharpe ratio purely by random chance (classic backtest overfitting). The authors spent a lot of time on this. They compared MadEvolve to other agentic tools (like Claude Code) and tracked how performance transferred from the training set to the unseen test set. Their key argument: if the AI was just p-hacking, the out-of-sample performance would flatline or decay as the generations went on. Instead, they saw a steady, parallel upward trend in both in-sample and out-of-sample curves, suggesting the LLM was actually discovering robust, generalisable trading rules.
What to Skim vs. What to Read

items: Read: Section 5 (the actual trading runs) and Section 7 (the p-hacking and overfitting analysis). This is where the real meat is for anyone trying to build systematic strategies.

Skim: The hyperparameter calibration details in the appendix and the background on computational cosmology (unless you really want to know how the same math reconstructs the initial conditions of the universe).

content.text: How to Use This at the Pub or in an Interview
If you want to sound like the smartest person in the room, here is your script:

The really interesting thing about the MadEvolve paper isn't just that they got a higher Sharpe on Bitcoin. It's the architecture. By separating structural search—which LLMs are great at because they can write creative code—from parameter optimization, which traditional math is better at, they solved the main bottleneck of AI-driven quant. The real takeaway is that the role of the quant is shifting. We aren't going to be writing the feature pipelines anymore; our job will be building the simulation environments and fitness functions so the evolutionary agents don't just exploit backtest bugs.

content.text: The MUM Effect: Why bad news gets sugar-coated on its way up

We’ve all been there. You’re looking at a spreadsheet or a project timeline, and you realise something is deeply, horribly wrong. The model has a structural flaw, the client is about to pull their mandate, or the software integration that was supposed to go live next week is actually three months away from being ready. Your immediate instinct? To keep your mouth shut, or at least 'soften' the blow. This isn't just you being a coward; it’s a well-documented psychological phenomenon known as the MUM effect.
What is it?

Coined by psychologists Sidney Rosen and Abraham Tesser in 1970, the MUM effect (Minimising Unpleasant Messages) is our natural reluctance to deliver bad news. We do it for two main reasons: we hate witnessing other people's negative emotions, and we have a very rational fear of the 'shoot the messenger' syndrome. Even when you had absolutely nothing to do with the disaster, humans have a nasty habit of subconsciously associating the bearer of bad news with the news itself.

In a steep corporate hierarchy—like an investment bank, a private equity shop, or a massive asset manager—this creates a dangerous game of Chinese whispers. A junior analyst spots a ten-million-pound black hole. They tell the associate it’s a 'minor discrepancy'. The associate tells the VP it’s 'under review'. The VP tells the Director it’s a 'rounding error'. By the time it reaches the MD or the CIO, they’re blissfully unaware that the ship is sinking. This is what project managers call 'watermelon reporting'—green on the outside, but bright red on the inside.
The classic finance example

Think of the legendary physicist Richard Feynman’s investigation into the 1986 Challenger space shuttle disaster. He asked NASA’s working-level engineers to estimate the probability of a main engine failure. They put it at roughly 1-in-200. When he asked the head of NASA, the big boss estimated it at 1-in-100,000. The MUM effect had filtered the risk so thoroughly on its way up the chain that top management was operating in an entirely different reality. In finance, this is how you end up with risk managers who are genuinely shocked when a portfolio blows up, despite the junior quants screaming into the void months prior.
How you can use this

items: If you’re managing people: You need to actively fight this. If you react to bad news with anger, you are training your team to lie to you. Instead, thank people for bringing you bad news early. A great phrase to use is: 'Bring me problems when they are small and cheap to fix, not when they are massive and expensive.'

If you’re the one with the bad news: Do not sit on it. Bad news is like fish—it does not get better with age. But when you deliver it, always pair it with a solution. Don't just say, 'The model is broken.' Say, 'The model has a formula error in cell X, but I’ve already run the corrected numbers, and here is how we can adjust the pitch to reflect it.'
Spot the 'watermelon': When a colleague or a counterparty tells you a project is 'progressing well but with a few minor adjustments,' start digging. Ask for the raw data, not the polished summary.

content.text: One line to remember
Bad news is like fresh fish; it doesn't improve with age, and keeping MUM only makes the eventual smell worse.
